At the edge of the city, where the streetlights gave up and the fields began, there was a bus stop with no routes listed.

Its sign was a plain blue square, faded nearly gray. Beneath it stood a bench that always felt dry, even after rain. People who found it by accident usually assumed the timetable had been removed by vandals. They would wait a few minutes, check their phones, and leave.

But once in a while, someone would sit down without needing to be anywhere else.

Then the bus would come.

It was never the same color twice. On some nights it arrived painted sunflower yellow, on others dark green, red, silver, or the pale blue of old photographs. It made almost no sound. Its doors folded open with a soft sigh, as if it had traveled a long way and was relieved to stop.

The driver never asked for money.

“Where does it go?” passengers would ask.

“Somewhere useful,” the driver would say.

And that was generally enough.

One winter evening, a woman named Mara found the stop while walking home from a job she had already decided to quit. She had spent eight years arranging flowers for hotel lobbies, weddings, hospitals, and funerals. Everyone praised her work. No one knew she hated flowers now—not because they were ugly, but because they reminded her how often beauty was treated like an obligation.

She sat beneath the sign with cold hands tucked into her sleeves.

When the bus arrived, it was orange.

“Where does it go?” she asked.

“Somewhere useful,” said the driver.

Inside, there were only three other passengers: an old man carrying an empty birdcage, a teenage boy holding a broken violin, and a woman asleep beneath a coat stitched with dozens of tiny pockets.

Mara sat near the back.

The bus drove past streets she recognized at first. Then it turned down roads that had never existed. The city fell away. The buildings grew lower, stranger, quieter. In one town, every house had a different clock on its roof, all showing different times. In another, people were sweeping last year’s leaves from a river.

Finally, the bus stopped in front of a greenhouse.

It was enormous, bright from within, and filled with plants Mara had never seen: black roses that glimmered like wet ink, vines with silver leaves, small blue flowers that opened only when someone laughed nearby.

The driver looked back at her.

“This is yours,” he said.

“My what?”

“Your stop.”

Mara stepped off the bus.

Inside the greenhouse, there were shelves of seed packets, each labeled in careful handwriting.

Courage, read one.

Patience.

Rest.

A Way to Begin Again.

She picked up the last packet and turned it over in her hands. It was warm.

When she looked up, the bus was gone.

For a long time, Mara stayed in the greenhouse. She watered what needed watering. She opened the vents before dawn. She learned which plants needed shade, which needed music, which only grew when left alone.

In spring, she began inviting people in.

The old man with the birdcage came first. He found a tree whose branches grew in the shape of open doors. The teenage boy arrived later and discovered a climbing vine that hummed in perfect harmony when touched. The woman with the pocketed coat brought strangers, all of them carrying something broken, unfinished, forgotten, or too heavy to name.

Mara never charged admission.

She only asked each visitor to take one seed with them when they left.

Years later, travelers began telling stories about a greenhouse beyond the city, where impossible things could be grown. Some said it was a myth. Others said it was a kind of hospital. A few insisted that, if you stayed long enough, you could hear the sound of an orange bus arriving somewhere far away.

Mara never confirmed any of this.

She was usually busy in the back room, pressing seeds into paper envelopes, writing labels in ink.

Not every packet had a name.

Some things, she had learned, needed to be planted before anyone knew what to call them.
